Behind every row: the Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee and the Advisory Committee of 1947, the Constitutional Adviser’s standing draft of 1946–49, and the Assembly secretariat. S. N. Mukherjee, Chief Draftsman, put

the Assembly’s decisions into legal form at every stage; Ambedkar told the House on 25 November 1949 that the ‘much greater share of the credit’ was his. He holds no cell because his work cannot be separated out
article by article — not because it was small.

text.tspan: These are two roles, not two ranks: neither is asserted to outweigh the other. Pioneer names the earliest Indian constitutional document that either stated the rule the article states or documented, in its

svg.text: own text, a clear intent to secure it — mere thematic resemblance qualifies as neither. It is a claim of priority on paper — not of originating the idea, and not of transmission: these documents drew on

older constitutional traditions, and the 1947 committees’ minutes cite foreign constitutions rather than any of them; the descent is established by comparing the dated texts. Framer names whoever is most
responsible for the words as enacted, on the evidence of a documented act — a draft, a memorandum, a minuted proposal, an amendment moved and carried, a formulation chosen. The underlying facts are
documentary and cited; identifying who shaped a text still involves judgement.

text.tspan: Collective or document-level attribution: the body is known, the individual within it is not. This applies to the Commonwealth of India Bill 1925, the Nehru Report 1928, the Karachi Resolution 1931, the

svg.text: Minorities Pact 1931 and the Sapru Report 1945, and to the committees named where the formulation was settled collectively and no individual act is recorded.

text.tspan: The Constitution of India Bill 1895 is attributed to Bal Gangadhar Tilak. CLPR’s remarks say that ‘Annie Besant seems to suggest that the document was influenced… [by] Bal Gangadhar Tilak’.

This chart is built backward from the words adopted on 26 November 1949. Each article’s enacted text was traced through the Draft Constitution of February 1948, Rau’s draft of October 1947, the Advisory

svg.text: Committee’s report of 23 April 1947, the Sub-Committee’s report of 16 April 1947, and the Appendices of ‘Clauses as Revised’ attached to the Sub-Committee’s daily minutes of 24–31 March 1947; floor
amendments and their movers are taken from the Constituent Assembly Debates, November 1948–November 1949.

text.tspan: As Constitutional Adviser, B. N. Rau drafted the clauses the Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee settled each day, and the minutes record the results as his — ‘Sir B. N. Rau’s draft of the clauses dealt with

svg.text: at yesterday’s meeting was approved in the form shown in the Appendix’ (25 March 1947). He had also submitted a draft of his own in March 1947, before the sittings — one of the committee’s two working

texts, adopted over Munshi’s at several points — which the minutes cite as ‘Document No. 4(ii)(b)’. His hand is easy to miss because the standard source, Shiva Rao’s Select Documents, prints the other

members’ drafts but not his; his text survives in the Appendices, in the minutes’ references to his draft, and in his own draft of October 1947. Where a row names Rau, his words are traced to one of the
two; where the committee or the Assembly changed his text, the change is credited to whoever made it.

text.tspan: The framer line credits surviving words, together with their documented driving forces and base-draft authors. Where the two still diverge the line follows the words: Article 15’s clause was decided while

svg.text: Ambedkar’s memorandum was before the committee, but the wording it adopted was Rau’s, drafted beforehand; Article 19’s selection of freedoms was Munshi’s but the surviving clauses are Rau’s; Article 24’s
subject entered through Munshi but none of his words survive. The full two-column record is in the report.

text.tspan: Article 22 is the only right with no pioneer. Article 17’s forerunner lies in the Minorities Pact (footnote 11), Articles 15, 18, 19 and 29’s in the adopted Karachi text (footnote 12), and Articles 26 and

svg.text: 30’s in the Sapru Minorities Sub-Committee provisions (footnote 13). Article 22’s rules — grounds of arrest, counsel, production before a magistrate — appear in no antecedent; their pre-constitutional
source is the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898, a statute, and they entered constitutional text only with Ambedkar’s article 15-A of September 1949.

text.tspan: By rows of this chart, the Nehru Report 1928 pioneers six (two by documented intent); the Karachi Resolution 1931, tested in its adopted text, six; the Commonwealth of India Bill 1925 five; the 1895 Bill

svg.text: three; the Sapru Report 1945 two; the Congress–League Scheme 1916 none — it has no bill of rights. The traditional chain survives with its weight resting on 1928–31, not on 1895.

text.tspan: On 31 October 1947 and again on 19–20 January 1948 the clause still read ‘without due process of law’. The Draft Constitution of 21 February 1948 carries the change in the Drafting Committee’s own footnote

svg.text: to draft article 15: ‘The committee has substituted the expression “except according to procedure established by law” for the words “without due process of law” as the former is more specific (c.f. Art.

XXXI of the Japanese Constitution, 1946)’ — the Japanese and Irish parallels are the committee’s own citations. No individual mover is named. The reason had been put before the committee by Rau’s report on

his tour: Justice Frankfurter ‘considered that the power of judicial review implied in the due process clause… was not only undemocratic… but also threw an unfair burden on the judiciary’, and Justice

Learned Hand thought fundamental rights ‘better… as moral precepts than as legal fetters’. Rau supplied the reason; the committee the words — and the row credits both, under the ruling that a documented
driving force is named alongside the body.

text.tspan: Alladi did not author the five writs of Article 32(2): Rau’s clause of 29–30 March lists four, quo warranto was added 14–15 April by an unnamed mover, and the writ names themselves are first in Munshi’s

svg.text: Note. Alladi’s documented contribution is ‘appropriate to the right sought to be enforced’, which becomes ‘whichever may be appropriate’. M. Ruthnaswamy’s credit rests on his demand of 17 April, which
contains the verb ‘propagate’, and his defence of it at the decisive vote of 22 April; the formal mover of Article 25’s three verbs is unminuted.

text.tspan: Names absent from the standard accounts: C. Rajagopalachari (Article 27, the shape of Article 17’s second limb, and the striking of ‘Slavery’ from Article 23); K. T. Shah (the rule of Article 18, ‘only’ in

svg.text: Article 23(2)); Alladi (Articles 16(3) and 16(5)). Also documented on the floor: M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar, C. Subramaniam, Syed Abdur Rouf, Guptanath Singh, Ujjal Singh, K. M. Panikkar, Mahboob Ali Baig,
Naziruddin Ahmad, Jaspat Roy Kapoor, Yadubans Sahai and Kala Venkata Rao.

text.tspan: Part III is Articles 12–35, and the study analyses all twenty-four. This chart shows the nineteen rights, Articles 14–32. The other five — 12 (definition of the State), 13 (laws inconsistent are void), 33,

svg.text: 34 and 35 — are the Part’s frame: definitional, enforcement and limiting machinery, a distinction the Constitution’s own group headings draw, since 12–13 sit under ‘General’ and 33–35 under no rights

heading. Their full attribution — including Article 13’s authorship (Rau, on Munshi’s topic) and Article 34’s documentary blank, presented with no recorded author on 14 November 1949 — is in the report.

text.tspan: Deletions are not credited: Alladi carried the removal of four rights on 19–22 April 1947 — secrecy of correspondence, freedom from unreasonable search, the pre-trial detention safeguards and the

svg.text: conscription ban — and Article 22 exists in the form it does because clause 28 was struck out. Failed proposals are not credited either. Hansa Mehta and M. R. Masani hold no cell: their clearest documented
act, a joint dissent for a justiciable uniform civil code, attaches to Article 44 in Part IV.

text.tspan: The Sapru Report (pp. 218–19, read at the page image) quotes Clause A of the Minorities Pact, presented at the Second Round Table Conference, November 1931 (R.T.C. Report, Second Session, Vol. 3, appendix

svg.text: 3): ‘The constitution shall declare invalid any custom or usage by which any penalty or disadvantage or disability is imposed upon… any subject of the State… on account of Untouchability’ — the earliest

Indian-authored text naming untouchability and stating a rule against it; the abolition of the status and the criminalisation are 1947’s own. The Pact was the minority delegations’ — Ambedkar sat for the

Depressed Classes — so the pioneer runs through their pact, not through any Congress document, and Ambedkar stands at both ends of the chain, 1931 and 1947. The Nehru Report 1928 nonetheless holds the cell

as documented intent: its narrative declares ‘untouchability is doomed’ and says of its rights clauses that they ‘will go a long way to remove the disabilities from which these classes suffer’, though the

clauses themselves state general equality and access rules without naming it. Clear documented intent qualifies a document as pioneer; on the same footing Article 27 goes to the Nehru Report, whose cl.

4(xi) bars endowing religion ‘directly or indirectly’. Intent must be documented in the text itself and aimed at the article’s specific subject — thematic resemblance does not qualify, which is why Article

text.tspan: The Karachi Resolution exists in two versions: Jawaharlal Nehru’s draft, and the resolution as adopted by the Indian National Congress in March 1931, which contains clauses the draft lacks. This chart cites

svg.text: the adopted text. Cl. 1(12), ‘The State shall confer no titles’, states Article 18(1)’s rule verbatim. Cl. 1(14), ‘Every citizen is free to move throughout India and to stay and settle in any part thereof,

to acquire property and to follow any trade or calling’, states the rules of Article 19(1)(d), (e) and (g), which no other antecedent reaches. Cl. 1(3), ‘The culture, language and script of the minorities

and of the different linguistic areas shall be protected’, states Article 29(1)’s rule — script included, sixteen years before Ujjal Singh supplied the word in committee. And cl. 1(4), ‘All citizens are
equal before the law, irrespective of caste, creed or sex’, documents intent for Article 15(1), whose enacted grounds add race and place of birth. Karachi’s document-level credit follows the study’s
convention: drafted principally by Jawaharlal Nehru, revised by Gandhi, adopted by the Congress.

text.tspan: The Sapru Committee’s own Minorities Sub-Committee (convener: the Metropolitan of India; report at its Appendix No. 2) proposed, in provisions the General Committee ‘approved the ideas underlying… but does

svg.text: not stand committed to the actual text’ (printed pp. 240–41): ‘All inhabitants shall be entitled to establish, manage and administer at their own expense, religious, charitable and social institutions,
schools and other educational establishments’, with free use of their own language and script therein and the right to ‘acquire, own, transfer, hold in trust’ property — the rules of Articles 26(a),

26(c)–(d) and 30(1). Among the ‘Special Rights… accepted by the general Committee’: ‘There shall be no discrimination with regard to the continuance or fresh allotments of educational grants-in-aid to

denominational institutions’ — Article 30(2)’s rule. Recommendation 17(d), read in full, adds ‘non-interference in religious beliefs, practices and institutions’. On documented intent both articles take
Sapru 1945° as pioneer, and the Sapru Report, the thinnest-sourced document in this chain, ends as the pioneer of two articles no other document reaches.
Compiled from the primary texts (Constituent Assembly Debates; digitised documents, constitutionofindia.net).
